Transmission Tariff (“OATT” or “Tariff”) is just and reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. 
Co-located load is addressed by the Tariff, which allows co-located load to acquire transmission 
service consistent with the Commission’s cost-causation principle. No Tariff changes are needed.  
I. 
BACKGROUND 
On March 22, 2024, PJM posted its since-rescinded Guidance on Co-Located Load 
(“Guidance Document”).3 The Guidance Document defines, and the Show Cause Order accepts 
for its purposes, co-located load as “end-use customer load that is physically connected to the 
facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the Interconnection Customer’s side of 
the Point of Interconnection (‘POI’) to the PJM Transmission System (co-located Customer 
Facility).”4 Although the Guidance Document recommended that all co-located load be served 
by PJM transmission service, the Guidance Document also contemplated that a co-location 
arrangement could proceed without procuring firm transmission service, in which case the co-
located generator would have to reduce its Capacity Interconnection Rights (“CIR”) to reflect the 
capacity designated to the co-located load.5 The implication of the removal of the CIR for the co-
located load is that those megawatts (“MW”) would not be available to the capacity market.6  
In Docket No. ER24-2172-000, PJM submitted an amended Interconnection Service 
Agreement (“ISA”) between PJM, Susquehanna Nuclear LLC (“Susquehanna”), and PPL 
Electric Utilities Corporation.7 The amended Susquehanna ISA would have implemented the 
Guidance Document’s option to proceed without firm transmission service as non-Network 
 
3 PJM, PJM Guidance on Co-Located Load (March 22, 2024) (updated April 17, 2024), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/pjm-guidance-on-co-located-load.pdf (“Guidance Document”).  
4 Guidance Document at 1; Show Cause Order at P 3 n.4.  
5 Show Cause Order at P 4; Guidance Document at 2-3.  
6 See Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Answer and Motion for Leave to Answer, Docket No. ER24-2172-000 at 
4 (filed July 10, 2024) (Accession No. 20240710-5036) (“IMM Susquehanna Answer”).  
7 PJM, Amendment to Susquehanna ISA, Docket No. ER24-2172-000 (filed June 3, 2024) (Accession No. 20240603-
5012) (“Susquehanna ISA Filing”).

4 
 
Load, relieving the co-located load of having to obtain transmission service. Although several 
commenters filed pleadings raising questions about the propriety of the filing,8 the Commission 
rejected the Susquehanna ISA because “PJM has not demonstrated that the proposed non-
conforming provisions in the Amended ISA are necessary deviations from the pro forma ISA 
due to specific reliability concerns, novel legal issues, or other unique factors.”9  
On November 1, 2024, the Commission convened a technical conference in Docket No. 
AD24-11-000 “to discuss generic issues related to the co-location of large loads at generating 
facilities.”10 Contemporaneously with that effort, Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
(“Constellation”) filed a complaint seeking to have PJM’s Tariff amended to incorporate the 
Guidance Document’s option to have a co-location arrangement without firm transmission 
service.11 The general thrust of Constellation’s complaint was that what Constellation calls 
“Fully Isolated Co-Located Load,” which it defines as “generation and end-use load co-located 
behind-the-meter in a configuration that includes protective relays to prevent the load from 
receiving power from the grid,”12 was not being served due to an asserted “gap” in the Tariff  
which allegedly renders the Tariff unjust and unreasonable.13  
NOVEC, among many others that reacted to Constellation’s complaint, protested the 
complaint, explaining that it should be denied because: (1) it would relieve co-located loads of 
having to pay any transmission costs even though they rely on and benefit from the transmission 
system; (2) granting the complaint would facilitate the withdrawal of generation from PJM’s 
 
8 See, e.g., Exelon Corporation, Protest, Docket No. ER24-2172-000 (filed June 24, 2024) (Accession No. 20240624-
5207); IMM Susquehanna Answer. 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078, P 85 (2024).  
10 Show Cause Order at P 5.  
11 Constellation, Complaint, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (filed Nov. 22, 2024) (Accession No. 20241122-5285) 
(“Constellation Complaint”).  
12 Id. at 1.  
13 Id. at 9.

5 
 
energy and capacity markets, undermining both markets; and (3) the subject matter of co-located 
load has broad industry-wide implications that should be addressed in a general Commission 
rulemaking, not in a company-specific complaint proceeding (if any changes to the Tariff to 
address co-located load are going to be considered at all).14  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission observed that there had been a “surge” of 
interest in co-location arrangements which has presented “significant and novel issues.”15 The 
Commission consolidated the Constellation Complaint and the Commission’s technical 
conference with the Show Cause Order proceeding so that the records from those proceedings 
would form a part of the Show Cause Order’s proceeding’s record. The Commission first 
addressed the jurisdictional issues.16 Turning to the PJM Tariff, the Commission determined that 
it may be “unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential because it does not 
contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and 
conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements,” explaining that “[t]he absence of 
such provisions may leave entities unable to determine what steps they can or must take to 
effectuate co-location arrangements of various configurations and how to do so in a manner that 
is just and reasonable.”17 The Commission expressed concern that without a common 
understanding of how co-location arrangements in various configurations will be effectuated, 
“participants in a co-location arrangement may not be required to pay for wholesale services that 
they receive, as required by the cost causation principle, which provides that all Commission-
jurisdictional rates and charges must ‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the 
 
14 See NOVEC, Protest, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (filed Dec. 18, 2024) (Accession No. 20241218-5285) (“NOVEC 
Protest”). 
15 Show Cause Order at P 65. 
16 Id. PP 66-73.  
17 Id. P 74.

6 
 
customer who must pay for them,’ and that costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least 
roughly commensurate with the benefits that entity receives.”18 The Commission also raised 
questions regarding the reliability and resource adequacy implications of co-location 
arrangements.19 The Commission posed a series of briefing questions to help it address the 
question as to whether the Tariff remains just and reasonable and, if not, what revisions to the 
Tariff would remedy those concerns.20 
II. 
COMMENTS 
 
NOVEC appreciates the Commission’s thoughtful approach to the question of co-location 
arrangements and respectfully submits these comments to supplement its protest in Docket No. 
EL25-20-000. NOVEC has no particular objection to co-location arrangements in principle 
provided: (a) that the co-located load obtains and pays for Network Integration Transmission 
Service (“NITS”) or firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service (“PTP Service”); or (b) neither the 
co-located load nor the generator to which it is tied are in any manner connected to the bulk 
electric system, either directly or via interconnection to distribution-level facilities that in turn 
interconnect with the bulk electric system. 
 
To summarize NOVEC’s comments below, NOVEC first addresses the question of 
jurisdiction. Next NOVEC explains why the specific configuration of the co-located load and the 
generator upon which that load is relying are of paramount importance to the Commission’s 
questions. Although there may be a variety of potential configurations, in the end the 
determination of whether co-located load or the supplier to such load should be required to 
obtain and pay for transmission service turns on whether the load and the generation serving it 
 
18 Id. P 74 (quoting Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004); citing Ill. 
Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009)). 
19 See Show Cause Order at PP 83-86.  
20 Id. PP 87-88.

7 
 
are both physically unconnected with either the bulk electric system or distribution facilities that 
connect to the bulk electric system. A co-location arrangement like the one advanced in the 
Susquehanna ISA or the Constellation Complaint did not involve such physically islanded load 
or generation and thus is not just and reasonable and is not permissible under the PJM Tariff. 
Such a configuration violates the Commission’s cost causation principles, undermines the 
Commission-approved PJM market structure, and is not fair to consumers. Third, given the 
historical cost-of-service arrangements for nuclear power plants that now, in part, make them 
attractive for these bilateral contracts, it would be unfair to dedicate such legacy generation to a 
single private customer after customers at large paid for such facilities and took the risks of 
construction since the time such resources were built. It is particularly troubling given the 
proposal and expectation that such units would remain interconnected to mitigate their 
weaknesses that require grid connection to operate -- thus deriving benefit from the grid -- but 
then be allowed to avoid paying for the benefits of grid interconnection. Fourth, NOVEC 
distinguishes behind the meter generation from co-location arrangements. Finally, NOVEC 
explains how the Commission may choose to integrate national security concerns into its 
decision-making processes.  
A. 
The Commission’s Jurisdictional Statement is Generally Correct, With Some 
Specifics as Applied to Virginia That Bear Consideration 
 
 
NOVEC generally agrees with the Commission’s statement on jurisdiction. Whether and 
to what extent a co-location arrangement falls under state or federal jurisdiction depends on the 
aspect of the physical configuration of the co-located load being considered, as well as the 
contractual and tariff arrangements and the laws of the state in which it is located.21 Under 
 
21 Id. P 68 (“As the comments described above illustrate, the boundaries between federal and state jurisdiction are not 
hermetically sealed. The application of these principles to the issue of co-location will often depend heavily on the 
specific facts and circumstances presented in particular situations.”) (internal citations omitted).

8 
 
NOVEC’s understanding of relevant state law, the co-location arrangements sought by 
Constellation in Docket No. EL25-20 would not be permissible in Virginia unless the supplier to 
the co-located load is authorized under state law to be a retail supplier in the geographic area in 
which the co-located load is located. Questions regarding the co-located load’s obligation or the 
supplying generator’s obligation to take and pay for transmission service in connection with their 
co-located arrangement is a matter of Commission jurisdiction.  
 
NOVEC respectfully requests that the Commission take care not to intrude on matters of 
state jurisdiction in the event that, notwithstanding these comments to the contrary, the 
Commission decides that some modification of PJM’s Tariff is warranted. FERC has jurisdiction 
to address PJM’s Tariff and transmission service generally, but matters such as the authority to 
provide retail service are within each state’s jurisdiction. Any modification of PJM’s Tariff must 
not infringe on the states’ jurisdiction over retail service. Further, NOVEC submits that given the 
complications presented by these jurisdictional concerns, the Commission should not create a 
novel contractual arrangement in the PJM Tariff that allows co-located arrangements to bypass 
transmission service, local distribution utilities, and the capacity market. If it does, the 
Commission risks creating an uneven patchwork of co-location rules across PJM as some 
jurisdictions permit it and others do not. 
B. 
PJM’s Existing Tariff is Just and Reasonable 
 
 
Implicit in the Commission’s question as to whether the PJM Tariff is just and reasonable 
is whether the Tariff should permit co-located arrangements in configurations that relieve co-
located load of transmission service costs or remove generation from the capacity and energy 
markets. On the contrary, the PJM Tariff is just and reasonable precisely because it does not 
permit that result. As discussed below, there are three reasons that support NOVEC’s position.

9 
 
1. Co-located load relies on the transmission system and should pay the 
same costs as other transmission customers unless it and the supplying 
generator are physically islanded. 
 
  
“Fully Isolated Co-Located Load” is not fully isolated if any physical connection to the 
distribution or transmission grid exists with the co-located load or with the generator to which 
the co-located load is connected. If there is any physical tie at all, even if there is switchgear in 
place to isolate it, the co-location arrangement benefits from and relies upon the transmission 
system. The benefits of, and the need for, the transmission system is the very reason co-located 
loads seek to maintain that connection to the transmission system and do not island themselves.22 
 
With respect to large generation assets interconnected to the grid, regardless of whether 
the unit is nuclear, fossil-fueled, or renewable, the grid necessarily responds to all power-quality 
issues caused by the generator or any load behind the generator, including but not limited to 
frequency response, reactive needs, transient issues, and voltage control.  Co-located load is akin 
to parasitic load because the transmission grid cannot differentiate between energy that is 
injected into the market and energy that is injected to serve co-located load. Additionally, nuclear 
powered generation units are not operated as flexible or partially loaded assets but instead 
operate at full load between fueling cycles to maximize the value of their fuel rods. As such, 
nuclear powered generation assets depend upon other generators on the grid to provide all 
ancillary service and other power-quality needs.  
The reliance is clear from the proposed configurations. As the Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners (“Indicated PJM TOs”) explained in their answer to the Commission’s 
 
22 See, e.g., NOVEC Protest at 10 n.35 (citing Large Loads Co-Located at General Facilities, Transcript, Docket No. 
AD24-11-000, at 113:11-17 (Dec. 3, 2024) (Accession No. 20241203-4000) (“And the final point that I would add is 
just that the grid has an immense reliability benefit that we are simply not interested in walking away from, and so we 
have every interest in getting the grid to be that reliability resource, and in that vein, at least from our perspective, we 
have no interest in diverting existing reliability grid connected resources away from the grid, thank you.”)).

10 
 
Show Cause Order, “all the arrangements being contemplated or requested as being 
interconnected with and synchronized with the transmission and/or distribution grid and thus 
[are] not ‘fully isolated.’”23 Because of this reliance, it is just and reasonable to treat co-located 
load as Network Load or require it to procure PTP Service. PJM charges transmission customers 
on a formulary basis without regard for the distance between load and generation.24 Thus, 
distance does not relieve one of the need to procure transmission service. 
 
PJM itself recognized that the co-location arrangement is still electrically connected and 
synchronized to the PJM Transmission System.25 It still uses various ancillary services at times 
to provide power quality products as identified in PJM’s response, including black start service.26 
It is problematic to NOVEC that certain co-location arrangements would still require black start 
service but are proposing to avoid paying for it — the availability of black start service to co-
location arrangements is indicative of the broader benefits provided by the transmission system 
during crisis. To the extent that a co-location arrangement is using the grid as a backup power 
supply, ancillary services, or other benefits, that is another way co-location arrangement relies on 
the transmission system. As the Indicated PJM TOs observed: 
 
23 Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Answer, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. at 9 (filed March 24, 2025) 
(Accession No. 20250324-5298) (“Indicated PJM TOs Answer”).  
24 Id. at 10.  
25 Id. at 12.  
26 Id. at 12; see also Exelon, Comments, Docket No. EL25-20-000, Attachment 1, at P 14 (“For example, there is no 
reason to believe that the data center load will be immutably fixed and, indeed, all load typically varies over time to 
some degree. To the extent the load varies from second to second, minute to minute, or hour to hour, it will require 
load following services.”) (Dec. 12, 2024) (Accession No. 20241212-5263) (“Weaver Declaration”); id. at P 15 
(“Likewise, the system needs to maintain adequate Operating Reserves (e.g., Spinning and Supplemental Reserves). 
Co-located load arrangements make no mention of how this configuration will maintain or provide such reserves from 
the nuclear units serving the data center should those nuclear units not be available for some duration—those reserves 
will instead be provided by generators somewhere elsewhere on the system to not only supply the location but to 
prevent the grid from collapse.”); id. at P 17 (“In addition, if the surrounding system was ever in a position of restoring 
the grid after a black out, it must rely on black start resources to support the restoration process. Nuclear units are 
incapable of providing black start services, so the co-located load must rely on black start services from other PJM 
resources on the grid to come back online.”); see also IMM Susquehanna Answer at 6 (“The co-located load will 
continue to rely on the grid for a range of ancillary services including frequency control, reactive, spinning reserves, 
reserves in general, black start, and PJM administrative functions.”); NOVEC Protest at 4-5.

11 
 
Moreover, in a recently submitted co-location arrangement and in the arrangements 
proposed and discussed in the Complaint, the co-located load depended upon 
another nuclear unit at the same facility for its backup supply of real power—which 
is to say, a PJM capacity resource that is interconnected with, serves, and relies 
entirely upon the grid. The proposed backup arrangement, including any 
“replacement capacity” mechanism, depends upon the delivery of energy from 
other locations on the network through PJM’s transmission system.27 
 
 
Co-location arrangements indisputably rely on the transmission system and its benefits. 
And, as the Indicated PJM TOs point out, all load, including co-located load, is used to plan the 
transmission system under the PJM Tariff.28 Co-location proposals that exempt co-located load 
from the costs of transmission service effectively give them free use of the transmission system 
and cause other load to subsidize that use. This is inconsistent with the Commission’s cost-
causation principle; the Commission should not approve free-ridership. The existing PJM Tariff, 
which requires co-located load to procure transmission service, is just and reasonable because it 
matches the cost of the transmission system with the co-location arrangements’ benefit from and 
use of the transmission system. The Commission should not order changes to the PJM Tariff, or 
if it does to clarify the provision of co-location services, it should still require co-located load to 
acquire firm transmission service. 
2. Certain of the proposed co-location arrangements have involved the 
removal of significant generation from PJM’s markets, which would 
cause an unreasonable and unsustainable increase in costs for customers 
even as the load causing those cost increases benefits from the markets’ 
planning functions. 
 
 
The Commission should be very concerned about the potential impacts to reliability and 
resource adequacy of certain types of co-location arrangements. If co-location arrangements like 
the configuration advanced by the Constellation Complaint are permitted, they will present 
reliability challenges. The Indicated PJM TOs explained that a Reliability, Availability and 
 
27 Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 14 (internal citations omitted).  
28 Id. at 14-17.

12 
 
Serviceability (“RAS”) system operation “may fail, thrusting the full burden of the co-located 
load onto the grid to continue operating if the co-located generation is offline for any reason.”29 
The Commission recognized the possibility that “if the generator were to trip offline, then load 
could appear instantaneously on the grid and cause serious grid level events at the scale of a data 
center.”30 The potential size of the co-located load only emphasizes the reliability risk — the 
Susquehanna ISA contemplated 480 MW being withdrawn from the grid which, under 
emergency conditions, could appear on the grid.31 Not only will 480 MW of generating capacity 
be withheld from the market as a result of dedicating that capacity to a single customer (the co-
located load), in the event of an outage of the supplying generation, the PJM system could be 
called upon to now serve that load even though it now has 480 MW less capacity in its arsenal to 
help it do so. If the Commission were to adopt a regime that significantly subsidizes co-location 
arrangements by relieving such load or their suppliers of the obligation to procure firm 
transmission service, there is every reason to believe that they would increase in both size and 
frequency.  
Any increase in frequency, if it means a withdrawal from the supply stack PJM can call 
upon, also presents a reliability concern. Reliability is assured by having adequate generation. In 
the event of a weather event like Winter Storm Elliott, where some generation becomes unable to 
operate, will co-location arrangements evoke Animal Farm, where some load, specifically co-
located, is “more equal” than other load? NOVEC recognizes that the Commission considered 
this question in its briefing questions when it asked: “Under what circumstances can PJM direct 
the operators of co-location arrangements to shed such load if deemed necessary to preserve 
 
29 Id. at 10. 
30 Show Cause Order at P 83. 
31 Susquehanna ISA Filing at 1-2.

13 
 
system reliability during a declared emergency?”32 If required to take NITS or firm PTP Service, 
the question will be answered — the susceptibility to cutoff for the co-located load would be the 
same as that of any other NITS or firm PTP Service customer. 
 
With respect to resource adequacy, NOVEC is gratified that PJM has rescinded the 
Guidance Document.33 Co-location arrangements organized along those lines present real 
resource-adequacy risks,34 and as PJM notes, is not permissible under the PJM Tariff without 
authorization.35 As NOVEC explained in its protest, “[t]he latest clearing prices for capacity in 
the Dominion Zone marked a 15-fold increase from the prior delivery year.”36 The capacity 
market has been constrained by lack of supply, which has already hindered its operation.37 PJM 
needs greater supply — as NOVEC’s Vice President – Power Supply, Mr. Jaramillo, remarked to 
the Virginia State Corporation Commission: “trends towards increasing levels of non-
dispatchable generation…may leave PJM wholesale electricity markets unable to provide the 
market-based generation NOVEC currently utilizes to meet the needs of its [data center] 
customers” and, even if generation is available, “increased costs in power markets may adversely 
impact all customers.”38 The capacity market sets prices based in part on supply: less supply

33 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. at 33-34 (March 24, 2025) (Accession No. 
20250324-5313) (“PJM Answer”). 
34 See, e.g., NOVEC Protest at 7-9; PJM Answer at 57 (“Depending on the configuration, co-location has the same 
implications for resource adequacy as load that is not co-located. These implications then impact the quantities of 
resources available to clear in the market and the resulting prices paid by customers.”) (emphasis added). 
35 PJM Answer at 57-58 (“All Generation Capacity Resources must offer their full Accredited Unforced Capacity into 
the capacity market, unless PJM has granted an exception to the must-offer requirement pursuant to the existing rules 
in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 6.6. While there is an exception from the must-offer requirement where the Capacity 
Market Seller ‘has entered into a unit-specific bilateral transaction for service to load located outside the PJM Region,’ 
there is no exception allowing Capacity Resources to not offer capacity bilaterally committed to serve load in the PJM 
Region.”) (internal citations omitted). 
36 NOVEC Protest at 8 (citing NOVEC, Opening Remarks of Gilbert D. Jaramillo, Case No. PUR-2024-00144 at 5:3-
6 (Dec. 9, 2024) (available at: https://www.scc.virginia.gov/docketsearch#caseDocs/145480) (“Jaramillo Remarks”).  
37 See Governor Josh Shapiro and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Complaint, Docket No. EL25-46-000 (filed 
Dec. 30, 2024) (Accession No. 20241230-5225). 
38 Jaramillo Remarks at 5:3-9.

14 
 
means the price increases. Co-location arrangements premised on generators removing 
themselves from the capacity market will only exacerbate the long-standing structural problems 
affecting PJM’s markets, as well as looming supply shortages.  
Moreover, it seems to NOVEC that, in significant part, the lack of supply arising from 
congestion in the interconnection queue, as-yet unresolved failures to act on existing 
interconnection approvals, and retiring thermal generation is the impetus for the interest in co-
location arrangements. Those supply problems affect all load, and it is discriminatory to afford 
some load a lifeboat in the form of co-location while the remaining load must address the 
consequences made worse by that lifeboat. 
 
However, there are co-location configurations that can maintain the integrity of the 
capacity market and are thus just and reasonable. The Indicated PJM TOs have already explained 
that co-location is permitted under the PJM Tariff so long as the co-location arrangement 
procures the necessary firm transmission service. In its answer, PJM discussed various co-
location configurations that are already permitted by the PJM Tariff and observed that “the 
capacity market was designed with such bilateral intra-PJM arrangements in mind, allowing 
sellers to offer such contracted capacity as ‘self supply’ into RPM Auctions.”39 Thus, generation 
associated with co-location arrangements is able to enter into bilateral agreements with co-
located load even as it satisfies its obligation to offer into the capacity market. 
3. It is unfair, and thus not just and reasonable, to consecrate legacy 
generation units funded by ratepayers to the exclusive service of private 
entities to the detriment of the public served by PJM’s markets. 
 
 
The Commission asked for comments on its question: “Finally, for generation units paid 
for originally by consumers in base rates prior to restructuring, is it fair and/or just and 
 
39 PJM Answer at 58.

15 
 
reasonable if these units are taken out of the system’s supply stack and devoted exclusively to 
serving co-location arrangements with one or a few large customers?”40 This is a legitimate 
question for the Commission to ask, one that neither PJM nor the Indicated PJM TOs chose to 
address in detail.41 As Chairman Christie emphasized in his comments at the February 2025 
Open Meeting, large load customers should be served, but it has to be done in a way that is fair.42 
 
The Susquehanna ISA and many other potential targets for co-location are nuclear power 
plants. They serve an important role in PJM’s energy and capacity markets and the PJM’s 
Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) has described them as “baseload power.”43 For the most 
part, nuclear power plants have the distinction of mostly having been built between 1970 and 
1990, prior to the restructuring of the electric industry in the PJM region. Thus, the plants were 
largely constructed by or for vertically integrated utilities who funded the projects from cost-of-
service rates collected by captive retail customers. This meant that it was retail customers who 
bore the enormous risks associated with the construction of nuclear power plants, where billions 
can be spent with nothing to show for it in the end. For an example, the Commission can refer to 
the expansion of the V.C. Summer nuclear plant which foundered after billions of ratepayer 
dollars were spent.44 Even a successful construction of a nuclear power plant can generate

41 PJM Answer at 72 (“This question goes further and asks about whether customers have an ongoing entitlement to 
units remaining as capacity resources based on their previous regulatory status prior to restructuring. Whether a 
specific cost is eligible for recovery is for stakeholders, the Commission, and/or appropriate state or local entities to 
decide.”); Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 21-22.  
42 See February 20, 2025 Open Meeting, https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/events/february-20-2025-open-meeting-
10022024 at 9:07-9:50. 
43 IMM Susquehanna Answer at 6; see also id. at 2 (“How will load be met if multiple base load generators are 
effectively removed from the market? What will the impact be on power flows given that the grid is built in significant 
part to deliver nuclear energy to load? What will be the impact on energy prices and capacity prices?”). 
44 Peter Maloney, Death of a nuke build: Summer abandonment leaves ratepayers holding the bag, UtilityDive (Aug. 
4, 2017) (Available at: https://www.utilitydive.com/news/death-of-a-nuke-build-summer-abandonment-leaves-
ratepayers-holding-the-bag/448597/).

16 
 
enormous cost overruns.45 The risk to retail customers was real, and the inability to assign that 
risk to retail customers in many areas of the country because of organized wholesale markets 
corresponds to the general end of the construction of utility-scale nuclear power plants in the 
United States. 
 
Since the restructuring of the electric industry, most nuclear power plants have largely 
been depreciated.46 Prior to restructuring, this would have benefited customers through lower 
rates, because depreciation is a significant contribution to rate base and thus the cost of service. 
If the Constellation Complaint were to be granted and co-location arrangements were to be 
allowed under that or a similar paradigm, it would shift all of the remaining benefit of that 
generation to the co-located load and away from other load that paid for that facility, all while 
also shifting transmission costs away from co-located load and onto the remaining load.47 
Although NOVEC agrees in principle that owners of generation assets should be able to seek to 
maximize the beneficial ownership of those assets, the Commission has the responsibility to 
reject proposals that are not just and reasonable because the Federal Power Act is a consumer-
protection statute.48 This is why NOVEC’s comments here are focused on incumbent generation, 
as distinct from new generation that is being or was developed to serve the co-located load and 
has not been participating in the market. NOVEC supports the development of new generation. 
 
45 Jeff Amy, Georgia nuclear rebirth arrives 7 years late, $17B over cost, Associated Press (May 25, 2023) 
(Available at: https://apnews.com/article/georgia-nuclear-power-plant-vogtle-rates-costs-
75c7a413cda3935dd551be9115e88a64). 
46 As an example of customers having already paid for nuclear power plants, many nuclear plant owners were provided 
accelerated recovery of the nuclear plants through a stranded cost mechanism.  While this process and the methodology 
for calculating the amount of accelerated cost recovery varied among the states, the result was that retail customers 
paid higher rates to fund such stranded cost recovery. 
47 NOVEC will also note that, to the extent that the nuclear generators received subsidies from federal or state 
governments, those were also borne by retail customers in the form of taxes.  
48 Xcel Energy Services, Inc. v. FERC, 815 F.3d 947, 952 (D.C. Cir. 2016) (“It is long-established that the ‘primary 
aim [of the FPA] is the protection of consumers from excessive rates and charges.’” (quoting Mun. Light Bds. of 
Reading & Wakefield v. FPC, 450 F.2d 1341, 1348 (D.C. Cir. 1971), cert. denied, 405 U.S. 989 (1972))).

17 
 
 
It is to the Commission’s credit that it appreciates the potential unfairness of the situation 
and asked the question. The Commission has periodically observed how the legacy of the pre-
restructuring period has created inequities and the possibility of unjust and unreasonable results. 
For example, in Opinion No. 494, the Commission found that the costs of legacy transmission 
facilities which were built to serve the transmission systems of individual companies and their 
customers could not be allocated to the entire PJM region under the Commission’s cost-
causation principles.49 The instant situation is the inverse, but it implicates the same principle. In 
this case, customers paid for the benefits of these legacy units, but the approval of certain co-
location arrangements that allow generation to withdraw from the capacity market would have 
the effect of shifting the benefits to private entities. Cost causation considers both costs and 
benefits of the service involved.50  
 
NOVEC respectfully urges the Commission to consider the legacy costs that retail 
customers bore before allowing private parties to dedicate the remaining benefits of existing 
generation to co-located load. The Commission should not permit any co-location paradigm that 
removes nuclear generation from the capacity market because it is not just and reasonable given 
customers’ investments and risk-bearing that helped make those plants now attractive to load that 
would now like to co-locate.  
C. 
There are Characteristics of Behind-the-Meter Generation That Distinguish It 
From Co-Location Arrangements That Warrant Distinct Treatment 
 
 
The Commission asked commenters to address how co-located loads are disparate from 
Behind The Meter Generation (“BTMG”) as defined in PJM’s Tariff or Non-Retail Behind The 
 
49 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Opinion No. 494, 119 FERC ¶ 61,063, P 42 (2007).  
50 Old Dominion Electric Cooperative v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“For decades, the Commission 
and the courts have understood this requirement to incorporate a ‘cost-causation principle’—the rates charged for 
electricity should reflect the costs of providing it…We often frame this principle as one that ensures ‘burden is 
matched with benefit,’ so that FERC ‘generally may not single out a party for the full cost of a project, or even most 
of it, when the benefits of the project are diffuse.’”) (internal citations omitted).

18 
 
Meter Generation (“NRBTMG”).51 There are differences that merit the distinct treatment. Unlike 
the co-located load which has been proposed up until now, BTMG and NRBTMG had or 
developed generation to supply the behind-the-meter load. In contrast, the co-located proposal 
here would not be relying on generation already dedicated to or that is built specifically to serve 
that load, but would instead repurpose existing generation from the capacity supply stack. The 
additional generation provides greater flexibility to customers and PJM, not less.  
 
In addition, the scale and subsequent impact to PJM of co-located load (which consists of 
energy intensive customers) relative to the scale and impact of BTMG should be taken into 
account. The Susquehanna ISA alone involved 480 MW. In fact, NRBTMG is currently capped 
under the PJM Tariff at 3,000 MW to ensure that it “does not detrimentally affect system 
operations.”52 NRBTMG is designed to make contributions to grid reliability during emergency 
conditions as well, whereas certain co-location arrangements would remove any obligation of the 
generation to support the grid as well as potentially exacerbate the emergency conditions or their 
underlying causes.53 Moreover NRBTMG fails to operate as required to support the grid during 
those occasions, the NRBTMG’s netting eligibility is reduced, which incentivizes efficient 
operation and availability.54

19 
 
D. 
If the Commission is Going to Incorporate Any National Security Concerns Into 
Its Analysis, It Needs to Explicitly Define National Security and Consider 
Countervailing National Security Interests 
 
 
The Commission encouraged “parties to address any national security implications 
associated with co-location arrangements, including with respect to the specific issues discussed 
in this show cause order, and what actions, if any, the Commission should take in response.”55 
NOVEC has several observations to offer. As a concept, “national security” has not been well 
defined in this proceeding. As Constellation used it in its complaint, national security is 
implicated because the failure to speedily adopt co-located loads will delay the development of 
artificial intelligence (“AI”) because data center generation will not be able to interconnect fast 
enough otherwise. But national security in the general sense is broader than AI: other industries 
are vital to national security — in particular, large industrial concerns. The price increases that 
co-located load could cause have the potential to harm their interests. Could that constitute a 
countervailing national security interest? One would think. One would also wonder about the 
existing data centers: they serve a vital function — does a cost increase to their operation harm 
their long-term viability and threaten national security? In an even broader sense, does the 
increase in costs to customers harm the general prosperity of the United States? If the 
Commission chooses to consider national security, it should consider it more systematically. 
Moreover, the Federal Power Act, in the context of sections 205 and 206, casts the 
Commission’s role as the arbiter of what is “just and reasonable.” Any consideration the 
Commission gives to national security must be as a component of a just and reasonable rate, and 
it cannot be a prime mover for the Commission in assessing rates.

20 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, NOVEC respectfully requests that the 
Commission find that PJM’s existing Tariff is just and reasonable.
